newsitem.title: USA: Second generation of poor families do better.
newsitem.headline: Second generation of poor families do better.

text.p: Researchers who followed children born into poor families through to adulthood said they found that early education was an important predictor of future success.

"Substantial proportions of inner-city children become successful adults," pediatrician Janet Hardy of Johns Hopkins University wrote. "Attention to improving public education, particularly language and reading skills, and the prevention of smoking and adolescent pregnancy are clearly indicated."

The study, which appeared in the journal Pediatrics, was based on interviews with the mothers of 2,694 children born between 1960 and 1965 in an extremely poor section of Baltimore, and follow-up interviews with the mothers and the children when the children reached the age of 27 to 33 years.
The findings showed 79 percent of the children graduated from high school compared with 28 percent of their mothers at the time they gave birth.

The children also turned out to be generally better off than their parents and 76 percent were considered financially independent. One in five of the children interviewed as adults earned less than the federal poverty level, compared to nearly half of the parents. But one in four of the children were later earning four times the poverty level.

Of the original children in the study, 82 percent of whom were black, 70 had died in the intervening three decades. About 40 percent did not meet the criteria to be considered in good mental and physical health, and 30 percent had a lifestyle that was potentially self-destructive or unlawful.
